lessons.title: Electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes

objectives: Define electrolysis, electrolyte, anode and cathode.
Predict the products at each electrode for molten and aqueous electrolytes.
Write half-equations for the electrode reactions.
Describe electroplating and purification of copper.
reviewNotes: Selective discharge rules are given in simplified form (less reactive cation, halide before hydroxide in concentrated solution); the Board's exact wording should be checked.
Quantitative electrolysis (Faraday) is not covered here; check whether it is required.

blocks.title: Electrolysis
blocks.md: **Electrolysis** is the decomposition of an ionic compound (**electrolyte**, molten or in solution) by an electric current. **Cathode** (−): positive ions (cations) move there and **gain electrons** (reduction). **Anode** (+): negative ions (anions) move there and **lose electrons** (oxidation). Electrodes are usually inert (graphite or platinum). Mnemonic: **PANIC**: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

blocks.title: Molten and aqueous
blocks.md: **Molten** compounds give the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode: molten lead(II) bromide → lead (cathode) + bromine (anode). In **aqueous** solutions water also supplies H⁺ and OH⁻ ions: at the cathode the **less reactive** of the metal and hydrogen is formed (hydrogen unless the metal is below hydrogen, e.g. copper or silver); at the anode a halogen forms from concentrated halide solutions, otherwise oxygen.

blocks.title: Common examples (inert electrodes)
blocks.md:
- **Brine** (concentrated NaCl solution): H₂ at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode; NaOH remains in solution.
- **Dilute sulphuric acid**: H₂ (cathode) and O₂ (anode) in the volume ratio **2 : 1**.
- **Copper(II) sulphate** with graphite: copper at the cathode, O₂ at the anode (blue colour fades).
- Half-equations: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

blocks.title: Uses
blocks.md: **Electroplating**: the object to be plated is the **cathode**, the plating metal is the **anode**, and the electrolyte is a salt of the plating metal (e.g. nickel or chromium plating of steel, silver plating of cutlery). **Purifying copper**: impure copper is the anode (it dissolves), pure copper the cathode (copper builds up). Aluminium is also extracted by electrolysis (see the extraction lesson).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Electrons flow in the wires, ions move in the electrolyte; solid ionic compounds do not conduct.
- Cations go to the **cathode**; anions go to the **anode**.
- With copper electrodes, the anode itself dissolves (the reaction is different from graphite).

blocks.caption: An electrolysis cell: the negative electrode is the cathode, the positive electrode is the anode.
blocks.alt: A beaker of electrolyte with two vertical electrodes joined by wires to a battery, labelled cathode (negative) and anode (positive).

blocks.title: Example 1 — dilute sulphuric acid
blocks.statement: Dilute sulphuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the gases and say what volume of oxygen is made when 30 cm³ of hydrogen is collected.
steps: Cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode: 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻. Hydrogen and oxygen are formed (water is decomposed).
Volume ratio H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1, so oxygen = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 cm³.
blocks.answer: H₂ and O₂; 15 cm³ of oxygen

blocks.title: Example 2 — brine
blocks.statement: Concentrated sodium chloride solution is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. Name the products at each electrode and what is left in solution.
steps: Cathode: H⁺ is discharged rather than Na⁺ (sodium is more reactive than hydrogen): 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Anode: chloride ions give chlorine: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain, so sodium hydroxide solution is left.
blocks.answer: H₂ at the cathode; Cl₂ at the anode; NaOH in solution

parts.explanation: Copper atoms lose electrons: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so the blue colour stays the same.
